passage: By October, Marek had counted it: every Friday Diego and the others found something new to try, from climbing the fence of the closed swimming pool to sneaking out to the railway bridge, and every time Marek said no thanks, someone made chicken noises. At first he laughed along. Then it stopped being funny. In the canteen in Gdansk he noticed Lukas and Ines, who had said no to plenty of things, and nobody mocked them for it. So Marek began sitting at their table and joining their Saturday bike rides. When Diego waved him over, Marek smiled and said, "Maybe next time for something else. See you Monday." Diego shrugged. It felt a little lonely, and also lighter than being laughed at every week.

How did Marek feel about the friend group by October?
qa.a: Marek felt worn down and no longer amused, because the mocking had stopped being funny, though moving away felt a little lonely.

qa.q: What could Marek try if Diego kept pushing, and why?
qa.a: Marek could keep the tone friendly but short and stay with the bike-ride group, since more time with people who respect limits makes the pushy group matter less.

qa.q: How might Diego see Marek's new seat in the canteen?
qa.a: Diego may feel puzzled or dismissed at losing Marek from the group, since Marek stays friendly but no longer joins.

grounding: Noticing that certain friends repeatedly pressure him and mock refusal, the student spends more time with others who respect limits, keeping a friendly but distant tone with the pushy group.

passage: In the hostel mess, Manoj's table was always the loudest. It was also where Thomas had heard "Don't be such a baby" more times than he could count: when he wouldn't sneak out after lights-out, when he wouldn't try the stuff someone's brother had sent, when he wouldn't ride on the back bumper of the bus. Last week, after he said no again, Manoj did an impression of him that made the whole table laugh. Thomas laughed too, and then felt sick. This week he took his tray to the far corner, where the quiz club lot sat. They talked about films and a physics problem. When he said he was skipping the Saturday night sneak-out, Arvind just said, "Cool. Want to watch a movie in the common room instead?" Thomas still waved at Manoj's table. He just didn't sit there any more.

qa.q: Where did the quiz club lot sit?
qa.a: In the far corner of the mess.

qa.q: What did Thomas feel after laughing at Manoj's impression?
qa.a: He felt sick and uneasy, having laughed along at being mocked for his own limits.

qa.q: What makes Thomas's shift a good balance?
qa.a: He moves toward friends who respect his limits while still waving at Manoj's table, keeping things friendly but distant.

qa.q: How might Manoj notice the change?
qa.a: Manoj might notice Thomas sitting elsewhere and feel puzzled or a little put out, but there is no fight to react to.

grounding: Shows a student noticing that one group keeps pressuring and mocking his refusals, and spending time with friends who respect limits.

passage:
Dear Vidya Didi,
You asked in your last message why I don't mention Nikhil's gang any more. The truth is I've been drifting away on purpose. Every time I said no to something, hanging off the train door, bunking to go to the dam, trying that vape, they'd mock me for days. "Mummy's boy." "Darshan needs permission." I used to laugh it off. Then I noticed I felt worse every time I went home. So I started spending lunches with Sunil and Faraz from the robotics club. They're a bit nerdy, but when I said I didn't want to go to the dam, Faraz just said, "Fair." No jokes. I still say hi to the old gang and play cricket with them sometimes. I'm just not around when they plan things. It feels lighter.
Your little brother,
Darshan

qa.q: What did the gang call Darshan?
qa.a: Mummy's boy, and said Darshan needs permission.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel going home after being mocked?
qa.a: Darshan felt worse each time, hurt and low, despite laughing it off.

qa.q: Why is Darshan's approach better than cutting the old gang off completely?
qa.a: Keeping a friendly hello and the odd cricket match avoids a fight, while staying away when they plan things protects Darshan's limits.

qa.q: How might Vidya Didi feel reading the letter?
qa.a: She may feel proud and relieved that Darshan chose friends who respect those limits 🤍.

grounding: A student's letter describes moving toward friends who respect limits and keeping a friendly distance from a group that mocks refusals.
